start/start: Training steps each weight against its gradient. But before the first step, every weight needs a value to start from.
start/equal: The simplest start gives every weight the same value: say, all of them a half.
start/same: Then every hidden unit adds up the same inputs with the same weights, and gets the same z: one and a half.
start/grad: Backprop hands each one the same gradient, so every step changes them alike: copies of one unit, forever.
start/symmetry: In 1986, David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams called this the problem of symmetry breaking: the units are symmetric, so swap any two and nothing changes.
start/random: Their cure: small random weights, so every unit starts out different.
size/randn: How big should they be? Code draws them with rand N: numbers centered on zero, with a standard deviation of one. Times a scale, the scale becomes their standard deviation.
size/big: Each unit adds up n terms, so z swings root n times as wide as a single term. A hundred inputs of variance one, at a scale of one, give z a standard deviation of ten.
size/flat: Through a tan-aitch, most of that bell lands on the flat ends: the units are saturated, with slopes near zero, so almost no gradient gets back.
size/small: So make the scale small: zero point zero one. Then z's standard deviation is ten times that: zero point one.
size/layers: Near zero, tan-aitch barely bends, so it passes that on, and the next layer shrinks it by ten again: one, zero point one, zero point zero one, zero point zero zero one. The signal fades away.
size/back: So does the gradient, multiplied by the same small weights on its way back.
size/lecun: Yann LeCun and colleagues warned of both in 1998: too large saturates, too small leaves the gradients tiny. They aimed between, for a z with a standard deviation of about one.
fanin/goal: A standard deviation of one keeps z on the bend of the tan-aitch, off its flat ends.
fanin/fanin: The scale that does it depends on n, the number of inputs a unit adds up. Drawn as lines, they fan in to the unit, so n is called its fan-in.
fanin/cols: In the weight matrix, each unit is a row and each input a column, so the fan-in is the number of columns.
fanin/rule: With inputs of variance one, z's variance is n times the weights' variance. For that to equal one, the weights' variance must be one over n.
fanin/std: So divide by root n: the standard deviation is one over root n. For a hundred inputs, one over ten: zero point one.
fanin/glorot: In 2010, Xavier Glorot and Yoshua Bengio studied why deep networks trained so poorly, and asked every layer to pass on the variance it receives: this same rule.
fanin/name: It carries his first name: Xavier initialization, the rule for tan-aitch.
relu/relu: A ReLU bends differently: it zeroes every negative z, and that is about half of them.
relu/half: Those zeros add nothing to the next layer's sum, so with one over n, its variance comes out halved, layer after layer.
relu/double: So double the weights' variance: two over n.
relu/he: Kaiming He and colleagues at Microsoft Research worked this out in 2015: a thirty-layer ReLU network that stalled under Xavier's rule trained under theirs. It is called Kaiming He initialization.
relu/shape: Try one: a ReLU layer, Kaiming He initialization, with a weight matrix of twenty rows and eight columns. Its fan-in is the columns: eight, not twenty.
relu/ans: Two over eight is a quarter, and its square root, a half, is the standard deviation.
